articles.title: Another rate hike seen
articles.description: ELEVATED inflation pressures and the peso hitting a record low last week could prompt the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to raise key rates by another quarter-point on Thursday. Nine economists polled by The Manila Times said the BSP’s Target Reverse Repurchase (RRP) Rate could be raised by another 25 basis points to 5.25 percent. The BSP’s policymaking Monetary Board, which has raised key interest rates three times so far this year due to above-target inflation, is scheduled to meet on Oct. 22. At its monetary policy meeting last Aug. 27, the Monetary Board decided to raise the BSP’s RRP Rate by 25 basis points to 5.0 percent. The interest rates on the overnight deposit and lending facilities were also adjusted to 4.5 percent and 5.5 percent, respectively. The central bank said the possible impact of severe El Niño conditions on agricultural prices pose further upside risks to inflation. Potential wage adjustments also warrant close monitoring, including their implications for broader price setting and second-round effects. Consumer price growth remained elevated, rising to 7.2 percent in September due to higher prices of key food items and energy costs. The September figure brought average inflation for the first nine months of 2026 to 5.4 percent, remaining above the BSP’s 2.0- to 4.0-percent target. Core inflation, which excludes selected food and energy items, likewise rose to 4.7 percent from 4.1 percent in August and 2.6 percent a year earlier. Jumbo rate hike likely Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. said the recent peso weakness, which hit P63.06 on Thursday, could strengthen the case for additional rate hike this week and in December meeting. “The magnitude of the rate hike next week will likely depend on the behavior of the peso in the coming days,” Neri said. “If the peso depreciates further and moves closer to 64, the BSP may consider a 50 basis point hike on Thursday,” he added. He argued that a larger hike could be viewed as “pre-emptive move” against second round effects and risks of de-anchoring inflation expectations. “Regardless of whether the BSP delivers a 25 or 50 bp hike next week, the balance of risks increasingly points to further tightening in the next 6 months,” Neri said. Sun Life Investment Management and Trust Corp. economist Patrick Ella said there was a 93.6-percent probability of a rate hike on Thursday, with a 25-basis-point increase seen as the most likely outcome. However, Ella argued that a larger 50-basis-point hike also remain a possibility. “Elevated inflation is the driving force behind this as core has climbed significantly vs September,” Ella said. Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. chief economist Michael Ricafort also said that the central bank could deliver another rate hike to help stabilize the peso exchange rate. Final hike likely Pantheon Macroeconomics chief emerging Asia economist Miguel Chanco said the central bank will likely opt to deliver a 25-bps rate hike only. He argued that the inflation rate last month “turned out to be relative to expectations” and this will be “the last increase, unless a new supply-side inflation shock arises.” Philippine National Bank economist Alvin Arogo said this could be the “end of the current tightening cycle as focus shifts to 2027.” He said they expect inflation returning below 4.0 percent by the third quarter of next year, but cautioned that the outlook remains vulnerable due to higher oil prices. “While our baseline assumes geopolitical tensions ease around the November US elections, a sustained increase in crude oil prices could still justify another 25 bps hike in December,” Arogo said. Chinabank economist Domini Velasquez also said that a 25-bps rate hike on Thursday could be the “final hike of the cycle.” “With the economy remaining weak, a lower 2027 inflation forecast and limited response of the peso to previous rate hikes could strengthen the case for October’s hike to be the final one in the current tightening cycle,” Velasquez said. Velasquez said that the earlier preemptive tightening could provide some buffer against second-round inflationary pressures. No hikes in 2027 HSBC Global Research senior economist Aris Dacanay said they expect the central bank to remain a “hawkish tone to rein inflation expectations.” “The risk of inflation breaking out of its cage is too large to ignore,” Dacanay said, which could prompt for more rate hikes. “We maintain our long-held view that the BSP will raise rates again in December, to 5.50 percent,” he added. “Though we have no rate hikes penciled in for 2027, the risk of a deeper tightening cycle cannot be ruled out,” he continued. Union Bank of the Philippines chief economist Ruben Carlo Asuncion also said that while growth and domestic demand remain soft, the central bank will continue to prioritize inflation. “We believe the BSP will prioritize anchoring inflation expectations and preventing broader price pressures from becoming entrenched,” Asuncion said. ING Economics also said that the outlook remains skewed to the upside amid uncertainty over “El Niño-related food supply disruptions, elevated energy prices, peso weakness, and potential second-round effects from higher wages and food costs.” “BSP is likely to err on the side of caution and maintain a tightening bias to tame inflation expectations until it’s confident prices are on a path back to target,” it said.

articles.title: Goldman Sachs sees Philippine growth picking up in Q3, but 2026-2027 pace still below targets
articles.description: The Philippine economy is expected to regain some momentum in the third quarter of 2026, although growth would likely remain below the government’s target as high inflation, a weak peso, and further interest rate hikes weigh on recovery, according to investment banking giant Goldman Sachs. In an Oct. 15 report obtained by Manila Bulletin, Goldman Sachs Economics Research projected third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 3.3 percent year-on-year, faster than the post-pandemic low of 2.3 percent in the second quarter. The government will report on the third-quarter GDP performance on Nov. 9. On a seasonally adjusted (SA) quarter-on-quarter basis, Goldman Sachs expects GDP to expand by one percent in the July-to-September period, also faster than the 0.6-percent quarter-on-quarter growth during the April-to-June period. The investment bank sees tentative signs of improvement in industrial production, sales, and commercial vehicle (CV) demand, although these are being partly offset by weakness in exports and residential construction as well as subdued credit growth. For the full year, Goldman Sachs forecasts the Philippines’ GDP to grow by just three percent, below the government’s already downgraded 3.5- to 4.5-percent target for 2026. GDP growth averaged only 2.6 percent in the first half of this year. The outlook improves next year, when the investment bank expects government spending to normalize while the gap between actual economic activity and the economy’s potential narrows. Still, its 4.5-percent GDP growth projection for 2027 would remain lower than the government’s also downscaled five- to six-percent goal for next year. Complicating the recovery is stubborn inflation, which Goldman Sachs believes will require the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to tighten monetary policy further despite lackluster economic growth. “The subdued growth outlook calls for a measured approach to further tightening, but we do not think it removes the need for additional hikes,” it said. Goldman Sachs expects two more 25-basis-point (bp) increases—one at the BSP’s monetary policy meeting this coming Thursday, Oct. 22, and another at its final meeting for 2026 on Dec. 17—which would bring the policy rate to 5.5 percent, from the current five percent, by year-end. The investment bank said weak demand may no longer be enough to contain inflation as underlying price pressures become more widespread. Headline inflation reaccelerated to a more-than-three-year high of 7.2 percent last September, ending four straight months of easing to remain way above the BSP’s two- to four-percent target range of year-on-year price hikes deemed manageable and conducive to economic growth. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy items to better gauge underlying price pressures, also climbed to 4.7 percent last month, with Goldman Sachs estimating that around 40 percent of items in the core consumer price index (CPI) basket were already posting inflation above four percent. Amid these pressures, Goldman Sachs raised its average headline inflation forecast for 2026 to 5.9 percent from 5.7 percent previously, and for 2027 to 4.5 percent from 3.8 percent, still above the BSP’s target band even next year. Goldman Sachs sees higher energy costs and El Niño-related agricultural losses as key threats to the inflation outlook, particularly as further crop damage could constrain domestic food supply. El Niño has already caused at least ₱6.9 billion in agricultural damage, while the investment bank noted that the strong-to-very-strong weather phenomenon is expected to persist until the first half of 2027. It also warned that sustained food and energy price shocks, together with peso depreciation, could eventually translate into broader adjustments in wages as well as prices. The Philippine peso, meanwhile, is expected to weaken further as the country continues to face a sizable current account deficit while foreign financing becomes less supportive, according to Goldman Sachs. The local currency closed at a record-low ₱63.06 against the United States (US) dollar last Oct. 15, breaching the ₱63:$1 level for the first time. Goldman Sachs noted that the current account deficit reached around 6.4 percent of GDP during the first half of 2026, increasing the country’s need for foreign financing at a time when overseas investors have been net sellers of Philippine equities and debt for much of this year. Inward foreign direct investment (FDI), which Goldman Sachs described as a more stable source of external financing, has also continued to weaken. Goldman Sachs said that if foreign capital is insufficient to cover the country’s financing requirements, pressure would fall either on the peso to weaken further or on the BSP to intervene in the foreign exchange (forex) market. Continued BSP intervention, however, would come at the cost of further reductions in the country’s forex reserves, the investment bank warned. It noted that gross international reserves (GIR) now provide import cover of about 6.4 months, down from around nine months before the recent deterioration. As such, Goldman Sachs expects authorities to exercise caution in using more reserves to support the peso so they can preserve a larger buffer against potential future shocks. The investment bank also noted that the Philippines’ real interest rate differential with the US—or the gap between the two countries’ inflation-adjusted interest rates—has turned negative. A negative differential means Philippine interest rates, after accounting for inflation, are lower than comparable US rates, which can make peso-denominated assets relatively less attractive to foreign investors. According to Goldman Sachs, higher positive rate differentials could help support foreign portfolio inflows.

articles.title: BSP rate decision, GCash parent debut to test local stocks
articles.description: Stock investors face a week packed with major market drivers, headlined by the stock exchange listing of fintech giant Mynt Inc. and the interest rate decision from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Market participants anticipate two central developments condensed into a short trading cycle: the market debut of GCash operator Mynt on Tuesday and the BSP's policy announcement on Thursday. Financial analysts broadly expect the monetary authority to deliver a 25-basis-point rate increase. Should the central bank act in line with market consensus, local equities are expected to hold their base above the 5,500 psychological threshold. While a successful equity debut for Mynt could offer a short-term boost to local market sentiment, market observers advise against aggressively entering positions ahead of the monetary decision. Brokerages generally maintain a cautious stance, favoring patience until monetary policy clarity emerges. Expectations for monetary tightening have mounted following recent headline inflation figures, which accelerated to 7.2 percent. The elevated price pressures are expected to act as a drag on local equity valuations. Analysts noted that a surprise pause on interest rates would be treated as a positive catalyst by equity markets, while a rate hike exceeding 25 basis points would likely induce selling pressure. Adding to macroeconomic challenges, the peso breached the 63 level against the United States (US) dollar for the first time last week. The slide marks another record low for the currency amid geopolitical tensions and persistent external headwinds. Foreign exchange pressures have been further compounded by persistent US inflation data, which pushed back investor expectations for rate cuts by the Federal Reserve. Simultaneously, elevated oil import expenses continue to widen the nation's current account deficit. Remittance growth from overseas workers—traditionally a buffer for the local unit—remains subdued, trailing below two percent for three consecutive months. Given relatively thinner foreign exchange reserves, market analysts warn that central bank intervention alone may be insufficient to halt the currency's decline. Consequently, the upcoming Oct. 22 BSP meeting carries a mandate to defend currency stability as much as it does to control inflation, making a 25-basis-point increase the bare minimum required to maintain interest rate differentials against the Federal Reserve.

articles.title: BSP rate hike seen certain, but weak peso raises odds of bigger move
articles.description: Private-sector economists watching the Philippines see the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) hiking interest rates by at least 25 basis points (bps) at its policy meeting on Thursday, Oct. 22, although the peso’s weakness has raised the possibility of a bigger increase. All 12 forecasts collected by Manila Bulletin from local and foreign financial institutions as well as think tanks last week point to the BSP’s Monetary Board (MB) raising the policy rate to 5.25 percent from the current five percent amid elevated inflation, a weaker peso, and risks of further price pressures. “We expect a 25-bp hike from the BSP and this is to continue to deal with elevated inflationary pressures, with pipeline pressures and second-round effects still heightened,” Singapore-based Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. Ltd.’s (OCBC) senior Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and India economist Lavanya Venkateswaran told Manila Bulletin. Inflation reaccelerated to a more-than-three-year high of 7.2 percent last September, ending four straight months of easing and remaining way above the BSP’s two- to four-percent target range of year-on-year price hikes deemed manageable and conducive to economic growth. “Although hiking won’t do much to fix the supply-side drivers of inflation, the BSP will be wary of maintaining policy credibility and keeping inflation expectations anchored,” Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) Asia-Pacific regional director Alex Holmes told Manila Bulletin. For its part, investment banking giant Goldman Sachs said that “broadening inflation pressures and peso weakness warrant further tightening despite subdued growth.” The peso closed at a record-low ₱63.06 against the United States (US) dollar last Oct. 15, breaching the ₱63:$1 level for the first time. Meanwhile, economic growth averaged only 2.6 percent in the first half of 2026 after gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by a post-pandemic low of 2.3 percent in the second quarter, way below the government’s 3.5- to 4.5-percent target for this year. Goldman Sachs Economics Research said underlying price pressures are becoming more widespread, as higher energy costs and El Niño-related crop losses could keep inflation elevated until next year. Goldman Sachs also expects further peso weakness amid a large current account deficit as well as weaker portfolio and foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows. Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. sees a greater possibility of a bigger BSP rate hike if the peso continues to weaken. “The depreciation of the peso beyond ₱63:$1 strengthens the case for additional BSP rate hikes, both [on Oct. 22] and in December. The magnitude of the rate hike [this] week will likely depend on the behavior of the peso in the coming days. If the peso depreciates further and moves closer to ₱64:$1, the BSP may consider a 50-bp hike on Thursday,” Neri said. “A larger hike could also be presented as a preemptive move against second-round effects and the rapid de-anchoring of inflation expectations, especially ahead of the potential supply shock from El Niño. Regardless of whether the BSP delivers a 25- or 50-bp hike [this] week, the balance of risks increasingly points to further tightening in the next six months. Under a more adverse scenario, the policy rate could potentially end the year at six percent if the Middle East conflict escalates,” Neri added. But British banking giant Barclays believes that a more aggressive 50-bp increase is unlikely. “While the BSP remains relatively biased toward hawkishness, we believe concerns over the sluggish economic growth outlook will restrain policymakers from unanimously endorsing a larger rate hike to quell inflation pressures,” Barclays Bank explained. Still, the combination of high inflation and a weaker peso adds pressure on the BSP to tighten monetary policy further, according to think tank Capital Economics. “A weaker currency risks adding to imported inflation, strengthening the case for rate hikes,” Capital Economics Asia economist Gareth Leather said. Japanese financial giant MUFG Bank Ltd. expects the BSP to maintain a measured hiking pace given below-potential economic growth and the 75 bps of tightening already delivered so far this year, even as elevated oil and food prices keep inflation risks high. “A hike would support the Philippine peso at the margin, but the inflation trajectory remains the larger risk,” MUFG Global Markets Research said. Whether Thursday’s increase will be the last of the current tightening cycle remains a point of disagreement. Singapore-based DBS Bank Ltd. sees monetary tightening continuing until year-end, citing further public transport fare adjustments, elevated oil prices, recent wage hikes, and the peso’s depreciation. “With inflationary pressures likely to be persistent, the likelihood of further hikes in the fourth quarter of 2026 rises,” DBS Group Research said. Dutch financial giant ING said the stronger-than-expected September inflation print shifted the balance toward an earlier rate hike in October. “The BSP is likely to err on the side of caution and maintain a tightening bias to tame inflation expectations until it’s confident prices are on a path back to target,” ING said. For Chinabank Research, persistent supply-side pressures from elevated oil prices, transport fare hikes, minimum wage increases, and the growing impact of El Niño warrant another policy rate increase, although weak economic conditions could eventually restrain the BSP. “Leading indicators point to a weak economy through year-end. As such, the October hike could be the final hike of the cycle, with earlier ‘preemptive tightening’ providing some buffer against second-round inflationary pressures,” Chinabank Research said. Philippine National Bank (PNB) economist Alvin Arogo also sees Thursday’s increase potentially marking the end of the current tightening cycle, although higher oil prices could change that outlook. “While our baseline assumes geopolitical tensions ease around the November US elections, a sustained increase in crude oil prices could still justify another 25-bp hike in December,” Arogo said. Singapore-based United Overseas Bank Ltd. (UOB) economist Jasrine Loke noted that despite the cumulative 75 bps of rate hikes since the war in the Middle East broke out, both headline and core inflation rose last September, with the latter climbing to 4.7 percent. UOB Global Economics & Markets Research expects the BSP to tighten “amid a more hawkish US Federal Reserve (Fed) backdrop.”

articles.title: Another rate hike seen
articles.description: ELEVATED inflation pressures and the peso hitting a record low last week could prompt the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to raise key rates by another quarter-point on Thursday. Nine economists polled by The Manila Times said the BSP’s Target Reverse Repurchase (RRP) Rate could be raised by another 25 basis points to 5.25 percent. The BSP’s policymaking Monetary Board, which has raised key interest rates three times so far this year due to above-target inflation, is scheduled to meet on Oct. 22. At its monetary policy meeting last Aug. 27, the Monetary Board decided to raise the BSP’s RRP Rate by 25 basis points to 5.0 percent. The interest rates on the overnight deposit and lending facilities were also adjusted to 4.5 percent and 5.5 percent, respectively. The central bank said the possible impact of severe El Niño conditions on agricultural prices pose further upside risks to inflation. Potential wage adjustments also warrant close monitoring, including their implications for broader price setting and second-round effects. Consumer price growth remained elevated, rising to 7.2 percent in September due to higher prices of key food items and energy costs. The September figure brought average inflation for the first nine months of 2026 to 5.4 percent, remaining above the BSP’s 2.0- to 4.0-percent target. Core inflation, which excludes selected food and energy items, likewise rose to 4.7 percent from 4.1 percent in August and 2.6 percent a year earlier. Jumbo rate hike likely Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. said the recent peso weakness, which hit P63.06 on Thursday, could strengthen the case for additional rate hike this week and in December meeting. “The magnitude of the rate hike next week will likely depend on the behavior of the peso in the coming days,” Neri said. “If the peso depreciates further and moves closer to 64, the BSP may consider a 50 basis point hike on Thursday,” he added. He argued that a larger hike could be viewed as “pre-emptive move” against second round effects and risks of de-anchoring inflation expectations. “Regardless of whether the BSP delivers a 25 or 50 bp hike next week, the balance of risks increasingly points to further tightening in the next 6 months,” Neri said. Sun Life Investment Management and Trust Corp. economist Patrick Ella said there was a 93.6-percent probability of a rate hike on Thursday, with a 25-basis-point increase seen as the most likely outcome. However, Ella argued that a larger 50-basis-point hike also remain a possibility. “Elevated inflation is the driving force behind this as core has climbed significantly vs September,” Ella said. Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. chief economist Michael Ricafort also said that the central bank could deliver another rate hike to help stabilize the peso exchange rate. Final hike likely Pantheon Macroeconomics chief emerging Asia economist Miguel Chanco said the central bank will likely opt to deliver a 25-bps rate hike only. He argued that the inflation rate last month “turned out to be relative to expectations” and this will be “the last increase, unless a new supply-side inflation shock arises.” Philippine National Bank economist Alvin Arogo said this could be the “end of the current tightening cycle as focus shifts to 2027.” He said they expect inflation returning below 4.0 percent by the third quarter of next year, but cautioned that the outlook remains vulnerable due to higher oil prices. “While our baseline assumes geopolitical tensions ease around the November US elections, a sustained increase in crude oil prices could still justify another 25 bps hike in December,” Arogo said. Chinabank economist Domini Velasquez also said that a 25-bps rate hike on Thursday could be the “final hike of the cycle.” “With the economy remaining weak, a lower 2027 inflation forecast and limited response of the peso to previous rate hikes could strengthen the case for October’s hike to be the final one in the current tightening cycle,” Velasquez said. Velasquez said that the earlier preemptive tightening could provide some buffer against second-round inflationary pressures. No hikes in 2027 HSBC Global Research senior economist Aris Dacanay said they expect the central bank to remain a “hawkish tone to rein inflation expectations.” “The risk of inflation breaking out of its cage is too large to ignore,” Dacanay said, which could prompt for more rate hikes. “We maintain our long-held view that the BSP will raise rates again in December, to 5.50 percent,” he added. “Though we have no rate hikes penciled in for 2027, the risk of a deeper tightening cycle cannot be ruled out,” he continued. Union Bank of the Philippines chief economist Ruben Carlo Asuncion also said that while growth and domestic demand remain soft, the central bank will continue to prioritize inflation. “We believe the BSP will prioritize anchoring inflation expectations and preventing broader price pressures from becoming entrenched,” Asuncion said. ING Economics also said that the outlook remains skewed to the upside amid uncertainty over “El Niño-related food supply disruptions, elevated energy prices, peso weakness, and potential second-round effects from higher wages and food costs.” “BSP is likely to err on the side of caution and maintain a tightening bias to tame inflation expectations until it’s confident prices are on a path back to target,” it said.
